newsitem.title: USA: Cuban exiles say Havana bombings are an inside job.
newsitem.headline: Cuban exiles say Havana bombings are an inside job.

text.p: Cuban exiles in Miami rejected accusations on Tuesday that they were behind recent bombings of tourist hotels in Havana and said the blasts were more likely the work of disgruntled Cuban government officials.

"It's obvious that in Cuba not everybody can get into a hotel, or have access to explosives," said Ninoska Perez, a spokeswoman for the Cuban American National Foundation, a hardline group seeking President Fidel Castro's ouster.
"So that kind of limits it to people within Fidel Castro's inner circle who have turned against the system," she said.
Perez said the bombings were the result of President Castro's refusal to introduce political change on the island.

A small bomb exploded on Monday in the lobby of the Melia Cohiba hotel, just three weeks after similar bombs damaged the lobbies of two other hotels, the Nacional and the Capri, in Havana. Another blast was reported at the Cohiba in April.
Cuba said the "terrorist actions" were organised and supplied by people in the United States.
But Perez and other exile community leaders said there had been no claims of responsibility for the bombings in Miami, home to the largest U.S. Cuban-American community.

"People here talk a lot...but I don't believe that anybody (from Miami) helped," said Tomas Garcia Fuste, news director and a talk show host at WCMQ, a leading Spanish-language radio station, who said he had heard of no claims of responsibility.

Cuba analysts guessed that the bombs were an organised effort, probably one that included top officials from the military or the interior ministry, noting the difficulty in Cuba's tightly controlled society of gaining access not only to explosive materials but also to leading tourist hotels.

"I dont think it's one person, I think it's a group," said Jaime Suchlicki, a professor of international relations at the University of Miami. "It's got to be someone who is in either uniform or from the security services, someone who can have open access to some of those places."

"To me...(the blast) is both an expression of political discontent and opposition with Cuba from elements within the regime," said Antonio Jorge, a professor of economics and international relations at Florida International University.

Cuba watchers also noted that the blasts on July 12 nearly coincided with the anniversary of the execution of Army General Arnaldo Ochoa. Ochoa, a much decorated officer who had led Cuban forces in Angola, was executed on July 13, 1989, along with three other officers on drug trafficking and corruption charges in a case that traumatized Cuba.
"This is maybe a reminder by somebody within the military that they are still kicking around and they are still pissed at Fidel for having executed Ochoa," Suchlicki said.

But observers deemed the bombings unlikely to bring about political change. They said the bombers might hope to scare off tourists, a crucial source of hard currency for Cuba's struggling economy, and send a sign to the world that dissent existed in Cuba.
But even Miami's fiercest anti-Castro exiles held out little hope the bombings would lead to any real change in the near term.
"Change cannot come as long as Fidel Castro is in power," Perez said.
